data.title: Whale Sells 47,900 ETH Worth $89.1 Million in Two Sales Within Days to Repay Loans
data.description: An unidentified whale sold 15,349 ETH at $1,701 each during a market decline, receiving $26.1 million to repay a loan in full. According to Odaily, Lookonchain reported that the whale had sold 32,541 ETH at $1,938 each for $63 million a few days earlier during a market decline to repay a loan on Aave.

data.title: Jim Cramer’s Investing Club Looks to Buy Advanced Micro Devices After 11% Drop
data.description: According to CNBC, Advanced Micro Devices shares fell 11% Friday, and Jim Cramer’s Investing Club is still looking to make small purchases when possible. The club’s portfolio director, Jeff Marks, said they are restricted from trading the stock because Cramer discussed it on television. The decline followed a report from short seller Hunterbrook Media alleging that a blacklisted Chinese company continued receiving AMD firmware that enables its chips to run in servers; AMD disputed the claims.

data.title: Bessent Says Anthropic Founder Will Make Large Donation to Trump Accounts
data.description:
According to Sina Finance, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a founder of Anthropic PBC will make a large donation to Trump Accounts in the coming weeks. Bessent gave no further details and did not name the founder, adding, “You will hear from their family soon.”

Trump Accounts were launched in July, allowing each eligible child to have a tax-deferred investment account authorized by the U.S. government. About 70 million accounts have been established.

Anthropic shares fell Friday, dragging U.S. stocks lower. The company completed the largest initial public offering in history earlier this week, and each of its seven founders now has a net worth exceeding $10 billion.

data.title: U.S. Data Center Construction Costs Surge 13% in 2026, More Than Double Global Average
data.description:
According to Sina Finance, Turner & Townsend’s latest report found that U.S. data center construction costs rose 13% year over year in 2026, more than twice the global average and about three times the average increase over the past decade.

Demand for large U.S. data centers has surged on the computing needs of artificial intelligence, outpacing the supply of sites with power access and construction workers. The constraints have extended project schedules and increased risks. The report covered more than 500 ongoing or recently completed data center projects across 62 markets and surveyed 400 industry experts worldwide. It said construction-cost inflation had stabilized somewhat but had not offset rapid growth in demand and project delivery activity.

Paul Barry, Turner & Townsend’s head of data center business in North America, said compressed schedules led contractors and subcontractors to include larger risk allowances in bids, covering acceleration, overtime, recruitment incentives and the risks of delivery on unusually tight schedules. He added that surging demand and pressure on supply chains had together raised overall construction costs.

A recent PwC report forecast global data center capital spending would rise from about $800 billion this year to $1.8 trillion annually by 2050. The U.S. is expected to attract nearly half of global investment in AI infrastructure, including data centers and chips.

In Turner & Townsend’s global survey, 56% of respondents cited power supply as a major obstacle to project delivery. Slightly more than half said utility-grid connections typically take one to two years, while nearly one-third said they take more than two years. For a standard 60-megawatt data center design, power costs were $15.01 per watt in Silicon Valley and $10.51 in Dallas. Slightly more than one-quarter of respondents said their contractors had enough capacity to clear their backlogs of ongoing projects.

Barry expects cost growth to ease to 6%–10% next year, saying many large projects have already started or are about to begin and that their contracts have priced in cost risks. He said a large wave of tendering and construction had arrived in 2026, with major projects already accounting for much of the demand.

data.title: TradFi News | Global Stocks Post Longest Losing Streak Since 2023 as AI Selloff Pushes Emerging Markets Into Bear Territory
data.description: Global stocks extended their slide on Friday, November 20, as confidence in AI-related trades broke down. The MSCI World Index fell for a seventh straight session, its longest losing streak since September 2023. The MSCI Emerging Markets Index fell more than 20% from its June high, putting it in a bear market. Asian markets, where AI-linked chipmakers make up a large share of benchmarks, fell hardest. Taiwan’s main index dropped 6.2%, South Korea’s Kospi 5.2% and Japan’s Nikkei 225 5.1%.Anthropic’s Record IPO Fails to Lift SentimentAnthropic’s IPO, the largest on record, did not reverse the pessimism. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the capital and debt poured into the AI boom can produce returns that justify current valuations. Anthropic shares fell about 10% to $87 in Friday’s premarket trading, just above their $83 offering price, a day after debuting on Nasdaq. Nvidia fell to $139, about 42% below its October peak.Investors Move Into Treasuries and Haven CurrenciesMoney moved into safer assets. US Treasuries rallied for another session, pushing the 10-year yield down to 5.01%. Bond prices are on track for their longest run of gains in five months.The Japanese yen and Swiss franc strengthened against the dollar. The US Dollar Index eased slightly on Friday to about 103.6 but is still on track for a fourth straight weekly gain.Gold and Silver Post Worst Week Since MarchPrecious metals did not benefit from the move to safety. Gold fell about 9% this week, dropping below $3,600 to around $3,555 an ounce. Silver fell about 14%. Both are on track for their largest weekly declines since March, as rising real interest rates hurt assets that pay no yield.Bitcoin also fell, dropping below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July.

data.title: AI | Rebecca Homkes Says AI's Job-Loss Impact Is Limited Right Now
data.description: According to Bloomberg, Rebecca Homkes, a lecturer at London Business School, said AI's impact on job losses is “quite limited” right now. Jobless claims continue to indicate that economy-wide layoffs remain low, even as companies increasingly use AI and automation to operate with fewer workers. Homkes discussed the AI trade and how the buildout has affected jobs and productivity.

data.title: Bitcoin News | Bitcoin Falls Below $60,000 for the First Time Since July as IBIT Posts Record $541 Million Outflow
data.description: Bitcoin fell below $60,000 on Friday, November 20, for the first time since early July, as a selloff in US tech stocks spread to Asia and hit crypto. It dropped to near $59,000 in early US trading, down more than 5% over 24 hours. That erases all of its August–September rebound toward $83,000. The drop followed a record $541.1 million outflow from BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) on Thursday, the fund’s largest single-day withdrawal since launch, according to Farside Investors.Altcoins Fall Harder Than BitcoinNone of the CoinDesk 20 index’s constituents traded higher. The index fell 1.9% from Thursday’s close to 1,644.31. Zcash dropped 11% and NEAR Protocol 9.3%. Tokens tied to onchain trading platforms, including perpetual futures, options and spot exchanges, were among the hardest hit, falling between 5% and 11% over 24 hours.Anthropic and SpaceX Slide Toward Their IPO PricesShares of the two companies behind the largest IPOs on record fell in premarket trading. Anthropic dropped about 10% to $87, just above its $83 offering price, a day after closing its first session at $97.17. SpaceX fell 6% to $130, below its $135 IPO price.Nvidia fell another 5% to $139, leaving it about 42% below its October peak. CoinDesk compared the decline to the early-2025 selloff; in 2022, the stock fell more than 60% from peak to trough. AI infrastructure stocks CoreWeave, Cipher Digital and IREN each fell about 5% before the open.Tech Selloff Spreads to AsiaSouth Korea’s Kospi fell more than 5%, with chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics each down about 6%. US tech index futures fell more than 1% before the open.Commodities Extend LossesGold fell as low as $3,515 an ounce before rebounding to $3,580. Silver slid to $41, about 66% below its January peak of $120. WTI crude fell 1% to about $82 a barrel, its lowest since August. The US Dollar Index eased slightly to 103.6.Traders Trim December Fed Hike Bets on Growth FearsTraders began pricing some chance that the Federal Reserve holds rates at its December 9 meeting, the first time in two weeks, as fears of an economic slowdown grow. A 25-basis-point hike to a 4.00%–4.25% range remains the most likely outcome. Markets have fully priced out a 50-basis-point increase.

data.title: Bull Market Faces New Challenge as Companies Shift From Buybacks to Stock Issuance
data.description:
According to Sina Finance, U.S. companies have shifted from years of stock buybacks to large-scale share issuance, adding supply to a bull market that has lasted four years. Acadian Asset Management said in a letter to investors this month that companies were net repurchasers in 2024 but have since become net issuers. Its latest analysis put net share issuance at 3.1% of total stock market capitalization as of the end of last week, below peaks during the dot-com and COVID-19 booms.

Anthropic’s IPO, priced at $83 a share above its prior expected range, drew strong initial demand, but the stock fell Friday and weighed on the broader market. JPMorgan data showed overall inflows into stocks and bonds remained positive; although 2026 data are not directly comparable with full-year figures, investor demand has risen as companies prepare IPOs and equity refinancing. Recent offerings included Oracle’s $10 billion common-stock issuance in November, Meta’s $12.5 billion mandatory convertible preferred-stock offering plan in October, Alphabet’s plan announced in June to raise $80 billion for AI infrastructure, and SpaceX’s June IPO, which raised $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their overallotment option.

A New York University Stern School of Business paper found that stocks have tended to deliver weak subsequent returns when companies favor share issuance over bond issuance. Lamont said the Baker-Wurgler equity share measure peaked at about 18% in 2021 and has risen again in recent months without reaching that high. Federal Reserve data also show bond issuance rising from 2024 and stock issuance surging in 2026. Lamont said companies had been net buyers of their own shares before 2026, but are now net issuers, and added that the possibility of an AI bubble cannot be ruled out.
